newsitem.title: USA: Fed sees moderate growth, no big price pressures.
newsitem.headline: Fed sees moderate growth, no big price pressures.

text.p: The Federal Reserve said on Wednesday that the economy kept growing moderately into the new year without any significant upward pressure on prices.
"Economic growth in December and early January was moderate in most parts of the country," the central bank said in the latest Beige Book report from its 12 regional banks.

The report, which was compiled by the San Francisco Federal Reserve Bank, will be used by Fed policy-makers to plot interest rate strategy on Feb. 4-5. They are widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged.

The Fed said its regional banks reported "scattered evidence of increasing wage pressures, particularly for skilled workers, but in general did not indicate significant price pressures other than for energy items."
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan made much the same point on Tuesday in congressional testimony that was widely seen as signalling that Fed policy is on hold for now.
According to the Beige Book, Christmas holiday sales rose by "small to moderate" amounts from 1995 levels and were in line with retailers' expectations.
Small-ticket items such as toys and apparel sold well, while consumer electronic goods fared poorly, it said. Price discounting was limited.
The Fed described the automobile market as "slightly downbeat," with regional banks in Phialdelphia, Kansas City, Dallas and Minneapolis all reporting slow December sales.
However, manufacturing industries "held steady or expanded in most areas." The strongest sectors were steel and other metals, machine tools, construction materials and capital equipment.
"In the high-tech sectors, semiconductor firms exhibited signs of recovery from a weak 1996, and computer firm shipments reportedly picked up following weak holiday sales," the Fed added.

Bank lending continued at high levels, although growth was generally limited. "Loan quality was reported to be good in most areas, except for concerns about consumer credit in some districts," the Fed said.
It described wage growth as "moderate" overall, despite strong demand for various types of skilled workers. No Fed district reported large year-on-year increases in wages.
Price pressures were also portrayed as moderate, with the exception of sharply rising energy costs.
Regional banks in New York, Philadelphia, Cleveland and Minneapolis characterised prices of manufacturing raw materials as stable.
Chicago said that upward pressure on construction costs has eased, but the St. Louis Fed reported that transportation firms were passing energy price rises on to their customers.
